explanation:
Operator overloading in C++ allows developers to define custom behaviors for built-in operators (such as +, -, *, etc.) when applied to user-defined types like classes and structs. This feature enables more intuitive and readable code by allowing objects to interact using familiar operators, effectively extending the language's syntax to work seamlessly with complex data types. It is particularly useful in implementing mathematical, container, or resource-managing classes where natural operator semantics improve code clarity and expressiveness.

Operator overloading in C++ allows developers to define custom behaviors for built-in operators (such as +, -, ==, etc.) when applied to user-defined types like classes. This feature enables intuitive syntax and enhances code readability by allowing objects to interact using familiar operators, closely mimicking natural language or mathematical notation. Proper use of operator overloading is essential for creating expressive and maintainable object-oriented code in modern C++.
example_explanation: This example defines a 'Complex' class representing complex numbers and overloads the '+' operator to enable addition of two 'Complex' objects, returning a new 'Complex' instance with summed real and imaginary parts. It also overloads the '==' operator to compare two complex numbers for equality. The main function demonstrates how these overloaded operators allow intuitive syntax for object operations, illustrating the power and clarity operator overloading brings to modern C++ programming.
